clinicalPearls: Combines the pigmentary and auditory features of Waardenburg syndrome with Hirschsprung disease (aganglionic megacolon).
Neonates may present with delayed passage of meconium, abdominal distension and features of intestinal obstruction alongside pigmentary signs.
Caused by variants in SOX10, EDNRB or EDN3, all central to enteric neural-crest and melanocyte development.
SOX10 variants tend to cause dominant disease with more severe deafness and can extend to neurological involvement (PCWH spectrum).
EDNRB and EDN3 disease may be recessive, with heterozygotes showing milder or isolated features.
Dystopia canthorum is characteristically absent, resembling type 2 in the craniofacial pattern.
The enteric aganglionosis reflects failed colonisation of the distal bowel by neural crest-derived ganglion cells.
Management is multidisciplinary, addressing surgical correction of Hirschsprung disease alongside audiological and genetic care.
reference.pathophysiology: Waardenburg syndrome type 4 is a neurocristopathy in which a single developmental defect affects two neural crest-derived populations: melanocytes and enteric ganglion cells. It is caused by variants in SOX10, a transcription factor governing neural-crest maintenance, or in the endothelin signalling pair EDNRB (the endothelin-B receptor) and its ligand EDN3, which are required for the migration and proliferation of enteric neuroblasts and melanoblasts. When endothelin signalling or SOX10 function is deficient, neural crest cells fail to complete their migration to and colonisation of the distal hindgut, leaving a segment of aganglionic bowel that cannot relax and produces the functional obstruction of Hirschsprung disease. The same deficiency reduces melanocyte populations in the skin, hair, iris and cochlear stria vascularis, giving the pigmentary features and sensorineural hearing loss shared with other Waardenburg subtypes. SOX10 is additionally expressed in Schwann cells and oligodendrocytes, so its variants can extend the phenotype to peripheral and central myelination defects. The absence of PAX3 involvement explains why dystopia canthorum is not a feature, and the mode of inheritance varies from autosomal dominant (typically SOX10) to autosomal recessive (biallelic EDNRB or EDN3).
additionalDifferentials: Waardenburg syndrome type 1 (dystopia canthorum, PAX3, no Hirschsprung disease)
Waardenburg syndrome type 2 (no dystopia canthorum, no Hirschsprung disease)
PCWH syndrome (SOX10 with peripheral neuropathy and central dysmyelination)
Other syndromic causes of neonatal functional intestinal obstruction
Congenital central hypoventilation syndrome with Hirschsprung (Haddad) overlap
Piebaldism or other pigmentary disorders coincident with bowel symptoms
additionalInvestigations: Rectal suction biopsy demonstrating absence of ganglion cells to confirm Hirschsprung disease
Contrast enema to identify the transition zone of aganglionosis
Audiological assessment including newborn screening and pure-tone audiometry
Ophthalmological examination for heterochromia and pigmentary changes
Molecular genetic testing of SOX10, EDNRB and EDN3
Neurological assessment and neuroimaging where SOX10 involvement is suspected
Family evaluation to clarify dominant versus recessive inheritance
redFlags: Neonatal failure to pass meconium with abdominal distension suggesting obstructing Hirschsprung disease
Signs of enterocolitis such as fever, distension and explosive diarrhoea in a child with aganglionosis
Severe or profound congenital sensorineural deafness requiring early intervention
Neurological features (hypotonia, developmental delay, neuropathy) suggesting SOX10 PCWH spectrum
Recurrent obstruction or feeding intolerance indicating surgical urgency
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends largely on timely surgical management of Hirschsprung disease and prevention of enterocolitis; with successful surgery and auditory rehabilitation many do well, though SOX10-related neurological involvement worsens the prognosis. Pigmentary features remain stable and non-progressive.
pitfalls: Overlooking Hirschsprung disease in a neonate whose pigmentary or auditory signs dominate the picture
Failing to recognise Waardenburg features in an infant investigated only for bowel obstruction
Assuming autosomal dominant inheritance when recessive EDNRB or EDN3 disease is present
Missing the extended neurological (PCWH) phenotype in SOX10-related cases
Delaying rectal biopsy and risking life-threatening enterocolitis
references: Paediatric surgery and Hirschsprung disease guidelines
management: Treat the associated Hirschsprung disease by surgical resection of the aganglionic segment with a pull-through procedure
Recognise and manage Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis promptly with rectal washouts, fluid resuscitation and antibiotics as an acute emergency
Provide early auditory rehabilitation with hearing aids and cochlear implantation for the often severe sensorineural hearing loss, alongside speech and language support
In SOX10-related disease, arrange neurological assessment, neuroimaging and surveillance for the broader neurological (PCWH) spectrum
Refer to ophthalmology and dermatology for pigmentary features with sun protection of depigmented skin
Offer genetic counselling addressing both dominant SOX10 and recessive EDNRB or EDN3 inheritance with cascade testing of relatives
Coordinate care through a multidisciplinary team including paediatric surgery, gastroenterology, audiology and clinical genetics
